claim: The LDL/HDL cholesterol ratio, mediated in part by CETP, is a major contributor to risk of atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease.
source: The LDL / HDL cholesterol ratio, mediated in part by CETP (Christison et al., 1995), is a major contributor to risk of atherosclerosis and coronary heart disease (Brousseau et al., 2004).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Christison et al., 1995 and Brousseau et al., 2004.

claim: Cholesteryl esters are a major constituent of foam cells in atherosclerotic lesions.
source: Cholesteryl esters, in particular, are formed from esterification of a fatty acid and cholesterol, are a major constituent of foam cells in atherosclerotic lesions (Ghosh et al., 2010; Yu et al., 2013), and, for certain lipid species, show a large difference in abundance between cavefish and surface (Figure 6).
evidence: This is stated with citations to Ghosh et al., 2010 and Yu et al., 2013.

claim: Inhibition of CETP has been shown to reduce cardiovascular risk, ostensibly by altering the partitioning of cholesteryl esters between LDL and HDL.
source: Inhibition of CETP has been shown to reduce cardiovascular risk, ostensibly by altering the partitioning of cholesteryl esters between LDL and HDL (Barter and Rye, 2012).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Barter and Rye, 2012.

claim: Lipid homeostasis in zebrafish exhibits strong similarities with human.
source: Indeed, lipid homeostasis in zebrafish exhibits strong similarities with human (Fang et al., 2014), and zebrafish express CETP whereas other model organisms such as mice do not.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Fang et al., 2014.

claim: Zebrafish express CETP whereas other model organisms such as mice do not.
source: Indeed, lipid homeostasis in zebrafish exhibits strong similarities with human (Fang et al., 2014), and zebrafish express CETP whereas other model organisms such as mice do not.
evidence: This is stated in the text.

claim: CETP and its cholesteryl ester substrates may be a locus under selection in cavefish to offset the risks associated with increased visceral fat.
source: This raises the question of whether CETP and its cholesteryl ester substrates may be a locus under selection in cavefish to offset the risks associated with increased visceral fat.
evidence: This is a speculation based on the observed differences in CETP expression and cholesteryl ester levels.

claim: Cavefish possess a significant reduction in certain long-chain fatty acid cholesteryl esters, particularly in peripheral tissues (muscle).
source: Cavefish possess a significant reduction in certain long-chain fatty acid cholesteryl esters (A–C) and cholesterol itself (D), particular in peripheral tissues (muscle).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6.

claim: Glutathione S-transferase rho (gstr) is consistently upregulated in Pachón cavefish.
source: Notably, glutathione S-transferase rho (gstr), a key mediator of glutathione antioxidant activity, is consistently upregulated in Pachòn cavefish.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Prdx3 (perodiredoxin 3) is elevated in cavefish.
source: Other genes such as prdx3 (perodiredoxin 3) and gpx4a (glutathione peroxidase) are also elevated in cavefish, whereas gpx1a, another glutathione peroxidase is upregulated in surface (but this difference disappears in wild populations).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gpx4a (glutathione peroxidase) is elevated in cavefish.
source: Other genes such as prdx3 (perodiredoxin 3) and gpx4a (glutathione peroxidase) are also elevated in cavefish, whereas gpx1a, another glutathione peroxidase is upregulated in surface (but this difference disappears in wild populations).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Gpx1a is upregulated in surface fish (but this difference disappears in wild populations).
source: Other genes such as prdx3 (perodiredoxin 3) and gpx4a (glutathione peroxidase) are also elevated in cavefish, whereas gpx1a, another glutathione peroxidase is upregulated in surface (but this difference disappears in wild populations).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (pck1/pck2) is generally upregulated in cavefish (although wild populations do not follow this pattern).
source: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (pck1/pck2), which catalyzes an irreversible step in gluconeogenesis, is generally upregulated in cavefish (although wild populations do not follow this pattern), whereas lactate dehydrogenase A (ldha) is upregulated in surface.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Lactate dehydrogenase A (ldha) is upregulated in surface fish.
source: Phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (pck1/pck2), which catalyzes an irreversible step in gluconeogenesis, is generally upregulated in cavefish (although wild populations do not follow this pattern), whereas lactate dehydrogenase A (ldha) is upregulated in surface.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Prolonged starvation decreases the capacity of fish to ameliorate oxidative stress.
source: Studies that focus on the impact of food deprivation on oxidative stress in fish show that prolonged starvation decreases the capacity of fish to ameliorate oxidative stress (Furne and Sanz, 2017).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Furne and Sanz, 2017.

claim: Glutathione is a major antioxidant that detoxifies ROS and thereby prevents cellular damage from oxidative stress.
source: Glutathione is a major antioxidant that detoxifies ROS and thereby prevents cellular damage from oxidative stress (Pompella et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Pompella et al., 2003.

claim: Cavefish show an increased expression of genes that are involved in the metabolism of glutathione in their natural habitat.
source: Indeed, in an earlier study we were able to demonstrate that cavefish show an increased expression of genes that are involved in the metabolism of glutathione, which is indicative of an increased stress level compared to surface fish in their natural habitat (Krishnan et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Krishnan et al., 2020.

claim: Reduced glutathione is elevated in the liver and brain of cavefish.
source: Here, we can confirm that these trends in gene expression are accompanied by elevation of reduced glutathione in the liver and brain (Figure 5, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Surface fish did not show a significant increase of glutathione in the fasted states.
source: We did not observe a significant increase of glutathione in the surface fish in the fasted states (Figure 5, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 5 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: ROS accumulation has been shown to cause lethal levels of cell damage in flies, but such damage can be prevented via oral administration of antioxidants or over-expression of antioxidant-producing enzymes.
source: ROS accumulation has been shown to cause lethal levels of cell damage in flies, but such damage can be prevented via oral administration of antioxidants or over-expression of antioxidant-producing enzymes (Vaccaro et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Vaccaro et al., 2020.

claim: Juvenile Pachón cavefish exhibit lower levels of ROS in cytoplasm as compared to surface under 30-day fasting conditions.
source: Using dihydroethidium (DHE) staining, we examined different populations and feeding states for ROS level. While liver sections of fasted / refed fish did not show differences in cytoplasmic / nuclear localization of DHE (Figure 8B–E), a quantitative analysis showed that, under 30-day fasting, juvenile Pachón cavefish exhibit lower levels of ROS in cytoplasm as compared to surface under the same conditions (Figure 8A), supporting the hypothesis that elevated antioxidants in cavefish may have a protective effect by neutralizing active ROS and may have arisen as an adaptation allowing cavefish to tolerate ROS produced by long periods of nutrient deprivation.
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 8.

claim: Elevated antioxidants in cavefish may have a protective effect by neutralizing active ROS.
source: Using dihydroethidium (DHE) staining, we examined different populations and feeding states for ROS level. While liver sections of fasted / refed fish did not show differences in cytoplasmic / nuclear localization of DHE (Figure 8B–E), a quantitative analysis showed that, under 30-day fasting, juvenile Pachón cavefish exhibit lower levels of ROS in cytoplasm as compared to surface under the same conditions (Figure 8A), supporting the hypothesis that elevated antioxidants in cavefish may have a protective effect by neutralizing active ROS and may have arisen as an adaptation allowing cavefish to tolerate ROS produced by long periods of nutrient deprivation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by the ROS staining data.

claim: Elevated antioxidants may have arisen as an adaptation allowing cavefish to tolerate ROS produced by long periods of nutrient deprivation.
source: Using dihydroethidium (DHE) staining, we examined different populations and feeding states for ROS level. While liver sections of fasted / refed fish did not show differences in cytoplasmic / nuclear localization of DHE (Figure 8B–E), a quantitative analysis showed that, under 30-day fasting, juvenile Pachón cavefish exhibit lower levels of ROS in cytoplasm as compared to surface under the same conditions (Figure 8A), supporting the hypothesis that elevated antioxidants in cavefish may have a protective effect by neutralizing active ROS and may have arisen as an adaptation allowing cavefish to tolerate ROS produced by long periods of nutrient deprivation.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary origin of elevated antioxidants.

claim: Cavefish exhibit decreased ROS abundance in the liver in 30-day fasted conditions, which correlates with the trend observed in glutathione.
source: Cavefish thus exhibit decreased ROS abundance in the liver in 30-day fasted conditions, which correlates with the trend we observed in glutathione.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the ROS staining experiment.

claim: Analysis of three separate transcriptomic experiments points to important changes in key genes, such as glutathione S-transferase, being consistently upregulated in cavefish.
source: Analysis of three separate transcriptomic experiments conducted by our group also points to important changes in key genes, such as glutathione S-transferase, being consistently upregulated in cavefish (Figure 6—figure supplement 1, Supplementary file 1-Table S2).
evidence: This is stated with reference to Figure 6—figure supplement 1 and Supplementary file 1-Table S2.

claim: Response to oxidative stress is an important factor in cavefish physiology.
source: Combined with the findings presented here, this suggests that response oxidative stress is indeed an important factor in cavefish physiology.
evidence: This is an inference based on the combined metabolomics and transcriptomics data.

claim: Antioxidant levels in cavefish may have evolved as a strategy to allow cavefish to tolerate variation in nutrient availability.
source: Antioxidant levels in cavefish may have evolved as a strategy to allow cavefish to tolerate variation in nutrient availability, as a means of controlling inflammation caused by deleterious energy metabolites, as a way of inhibiting atherogenesis, or several of these effects.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary role of antioxidants in cavefish.

claim: Antioxidant levels in cavefish may have evolved as a means of controlling inflammation caused by deleterious energy metabolites.
source: Antioxidant levels in cavefish may have evolved as a strategy to allow cavefish to tolerate variation in nutrient availability, as a means of controlling inflammation caused by deleterious energy metabolites, as a way of inhibiting atherogenesis, or several of these effects.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary role of antioxidants in cavefish.

claim: Antioxidant levels in cavefish may have evolved as a way of inhibiting atherogenesis.
source: Antioxidant levels in cavefish may have evolved as a strategy to allow cavefish to tolerate variation in nutrient availability, as a means of controlling inflammation caused by deleterious energy metabolites, as a way of inhibiting atherogenesis, or several of these effects.
evidence: This is a speculation about the evolutionary role of antioxidants in cavefish.

claim: Cavefish appear to have substantially altered sugar metabolism, and exhibit higher levels of sugars and sugar phosphates.
source: We found that drastic alterations in energy metabolism, together with shifts in mediators of redox metabolism and ascorbate, an essential vitamin which is lacking in the cave environment, constitute a major feature of cave adaptation in these populations. Cavefish appear to have substantially altered sugar metabolism, and exhibit higher levels of sugars and sugar phosphates.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolomics analysis.

claim: The opposite trend occurs for uronic acids, which are the oxidized forms of simple reducing sugars.
source: However, the opposite trend occurs for uronic acids, which are the oxidized forms of simple reducing sugars and can be formed enzymatically or non-enzymatically.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolomics analysis.

claim: There is an overall trend to decreased reliance on oxidative metabolism and increased reliance on sugar metabolism in cavefish.
source: This incongruency can be resolved by noting the overall trend to decreased reliance on oxidative metabolism (and enzymes that catalyze oxidative processes) and increased reliance on sugar metabolism.
evidence: This is an inference based on the metabolomics data.

claim: The specific reduction of uronic acids may have an additional survival benefit for cavefish by inhibiting protein glycation and thus preventing accumulation of advanced glycation end products.
source: However, the specific reduction of uronic acids in particular may have an additional survival benefit for cavefish by inhibiting protein glycation and thus preventing accumulation of advanced glycation end products.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of reduced uronic acids.

claim: Upregulation of glucose and long-chain fatty acid production is a common feature shared by Pachón and Tinaja cave populations.
source: Our data indicate that upregulation of glucose and long-chain fatty acid production is a common feature shared by Pachón and Tinaja cave populations, suggesting that certain cave habitats do require considerable changes in energy metabolism.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the metabolomics analysis.

claim: Pachón and Tinaja likely have a greater reliance on fat stores for locomotion, as evidenced by increased SFA content in muscle in fasting and refeeding.
source: Pachón and Tinaja likely have a greater reliance on fat stores for locomotion, as evidenced by increased SFA content in muscle in fasting and refeeding.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased SFA content in muscle.

claim: A. mexicanus troglomorphic populations share many metabolic similarities with known pathological conditions such as obesity.
source: In summary, A. mexicanus troglomorphic populations share many metabolic similarities with known pathological conditions such as obesity, but also display important differences which may help to explain their resistance to negative effects of these pathologies.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: A. mexicanus troglomorphic populations display important differences from pathological conditions which may help to explain their resistance to negative effects of these pathologies.
source: In summary, A. mexicanus troglomorphic populations share many metabolic similarities with known pathological conditions such as obesity, but also display important differences which may help to explain their resistance to negative effects of these pathologies.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of the findings.

claim: Pachón cavefish possess lower levels of superoxide radicals in the liver after 30 days of fasting.
source: We have shown via ROS staining that Pachòn cavefish do possess lower levels of superoxide radicals in the liver after 30 days of fasting.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the ROS staining experiment.

claim: Increased antioxidant levels in cavefish correlate with physiological state.
source: This confirms that increased antioxide levels in cavefish do indeed correlate with physiological state, and suggests that selection in cave environments favors resistance to oxidative stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the ROS staining and metabolomics data.

claim: Selection in cave environments favors resistance to oxidative stress.
source: This confirms that increased antioxide levels in cavefish do indeed correlate with physiological state, and suggests that selection in cave environments favors resistance to oxidative stress.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed antioxidant levels and ROS data.

claim: A. mexicanus cave populations exhibit altered lipoprotein composition and expression of CETP.
source: A. mexicanus cave populations clearly exhibit altered lipoprotein composition and expression of CETP, an important component of lipid homeostasis.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the study.

claim: Altered lipoprotein composition and CETP expression, together with increased abundance of antioxidants, may contribute to the ability of cavefish to withstand high triglyceride levels.
source: Together with increased abundance of antioxidants, this may contribute to the ability of cavefish to withstand high triglyceride levels.
evidence: This is a speculation about the functional significance of the observed metabolic changes.

claim: The analysis was based on juvenile, pre-sexually mature fish.
source: However, there are limitations to our approach. Our analysis was based on juvenile, pre-sexually mature fish.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: An age of 5 months does not necessarily coincide with seasonally-correlated food shortages.
source: However, an age of 5 months does not necessarily coincide with seasonally-correlated food shortages, and hence manifestations of starvation adaptations may not occur until a later developmental stage.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: The study did not examine a fasting duration of greater than 1 month.
source: We also did not examine a fasting duration of greater than 1 month, despite the potential for longer periods of nutrient deprivation in cave environments.
evidence: This is stated as a limitation of the study.

claim: Certain health effects, particularly cardiovascular disease, can be predicted from metabolic signatures prior to clinical manifestations.
source: Recent work (Cirulli et al., 2019) has shown that certain health effects, particularly cardiovascular disease, can be predicted from metabolic signatures prior to clinical manifestations.
evidence: This is stated with citation to Cirulli et al., 2019.

claim: Metabolic dysregulation has causal influence over the disease state of an organism.
source: This suggests that metabolic dysregulation has causal influence over the disease state of an organism, and conversely disease may be preventable via metabolic intervention (Rubino et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Rubino et al., 2016.

claim: Disease may be preventable via metabolic intervention.
source: This suggests that metabolic dysregulation has causal influence over the disease state of an organism, and conversely disease may be preventable via metabolic intervention (Rubino et al., 2016).
